content:
Quantum computing is often seen as a technology of the future, but not every quantum application requires waiting for a powerful computer capable of solving problems that cannot be tackled today. Quantum X Labs (QXL), an Israeli quantum technology company listed on Nasdaq, operates in three areas: quantum computer development, quantum sensing, and applications that combine classical and quantum computing. One of its most intriguing developments in quantum sensing is a next-generation compass designed to enable precise navigation even without GPS.

The need for such a system extends beyond the battlefield. Autonomous vehicles, robots, and military platforms require reliable positioning data even in areas where satellite signals are unavailable or jammed. “Autonomous cars navigate primarily using GPS. It’s an excellent system, but we saw during the recent war how easily it can be disrupted,” says Prof. Nir Sharon, QXL’s co-founder and CTO. The sensor the company is developing is designed to operate alongside GPS and continue providing positioning information when satellite reception is lost.

To explain the significance of this improvement, Sharon looks back at the history of navigation. For centuries, seafarers relied on magnetic compasses, which provided a sense of direction but were limited in their accuracy. Missions to the Moon required a different kind of compass: an electric compass, which was far more accurate than its magnetic predecessor and enabled more precise navigation and control in space. QXL now aims to take the technology a step further. “The device we know how to build represents the next leap: an improvement of four, five, or even more orders of magnitude over what can be achieved today, in a very small device,” Sharon says. Greater accuracy allows the system to continue calculating its position over time without accumulated drift becoming significant. Beyond vehicles, potential applications include robots and other platforms that need to know precisely where they are.

The compass is part of quantum sensing, one of the company’s three areas of activity. Alongside its development, QXL is working on highly accurate atomic clocks and additional sensors. “Sensing gets somewhat less attention and is seen as less flashy, but it is a very interesting field, particularly in defense-related contexts,” Sharon says. Such sensors could be used in navigation and communications systems, and some of the company's developments are already operational. “We are already at the point where some things are working and are expected to become products in the foreseeable future.”

At the same time, the company is developing a quantum computer based on laser-controlled cold atoms, one of the leading architectures in the field. It is also working on software for quantum error correction. Unlike classical computers, where systems from different manufacturers are relatively similar, quantum computing has yet to settle on a standard architecture. “There is still no standard for quantum computers. Every company building one chooses the model it believes in and the capabilities it can deliver, and each approach has its advantages and disadvantages.”

The company’s third area focuses on applications that combine classical and quantum computing to tackle problems that existing systems struggle to solve. QXL is exploring opportunities in information security, clinical trials and pharmaceuticals, as well as simulations.

Securing quantum computers, not just defending against them

In cybersecurity, much of the industry is focused on preparing for the Harvest Now, Decrypt Later threat: collecting encrypted information today with the intention of decrypting it in the future using quantum computers. QXL has chosen a different direction: securing quantum computers themselves and future quantum communication channels.

“Quantum computers operate in a fundamentally different way from conventional computers, and their operating principles create new threats that need to be addressed,” Sharon explains. One concern involves information exposed while a quantum algorithm is running. For example, when a user runs a computation on a cloud-based quantum computer, the question arises of how to protect that user's information during processing.

Another challenge is protecting the algorithms themselves and the unique parameters on which they are based. Sharon compares this to artificial intelligence models, where the parameters created during training account for a significant part of a model’s value. “These parameters are often the result of intensive learning that requires many hours, energy, and money.” QXL is developing solutions to authenticate algorithms and protect their intellectual property, helping prevent unauthorized copying or use.

The company also has ties to organizations in the defense industry, and some of its products are intended for defense applications. Former Mossad chief Yossi Cohen heads its scientific committee. Sharon emphasizes that, for a relatively small company operating in a complex market, understanding the industry and its customers’ needs is just as important as technological expertise. “We need people who can help us open doors, explain who we should work with and who we shouldn’t, and provide the right input. That is a very significant added value.”

QXL also collaborates with companies such as Nvidia and IBM. These partnerships help it improve its products, understand its partners’ needs, and exchange knowledge and ideas with experts in the field. “Working alone in such a technological, scientific, and knowledge-intensive field simply isn’t the right approach,” Sharon says. He notes that Israel’s quantum industry has retained a collaborative culture rooted in academia, although commercial secrets and patents naturally remain part of the picture.

Where will quantum computing really have the edge?

One of the central questions facing the quantum computing industry is where, exactly, a quantum computer will offer the greatest advantage: which tasks it will be able to complement classical computing and AI in, and which it may be able to perform better. Sharon calls this “the holy grail of the entire industry.”

QXL is exploring computational methods and algorithms to identify where a genuine quantum advantage exists. Some projects have already moved beyond the research-testing stage, but in others, particularly in software, the final product is not yet clear. The company continues to explore possibilities, build expertise, and advance its technology, but Sharon stresses that it is still too early to promise when these solutions will be ready for practical use.
